paragraphs: Nashville wrote its first data center zoning rules in July 2026, driven by opposition to two proposals. On July 21 the Metro Council passed BL2026-1391, banning data centers larger than 500,000 square feet anywhere in Davidson County, requiring smaller ones to get a special exception after a public hearing, limiting large facilities to land already zoned heavy industrial, and keeping them half a mile from schools, homes and parks. The same night the council passed a temporary moratorium on new data center construction, running through December 1.

The fight that drove the vote is DC Blox's plan for a 50-megawatt data center in two buildings on more than 23 acres next to the Nashville Zoo, which it bought for $23 million in July. A petition against it passed half a million signatures. Metro's zoning administrator ruled the new rules did not apply because DC Blox had already applied for permits under Tennessee's vested rights law. Mayor Freddie O'Connell then asked the council for authority to take the land; it voted 27-5 on August 4 to let city attorneys start eminent domain proceedings. On August 11, DC Blox sued Metro in federal court, calling the moratorium "a targeted attack against DC BLOX."

The other proposal is at Fisk University, the historically Black university in North Nashville, which announced in May a 30-megawatt data center as part of a campus master plan. Developer Don Hardin said Fisk would not need all that power itself; neighbor Kaylynn Mourning, who started a petition against it, said it "could mean higher electric bills, unsafe drinking water, pollution."

A TVA spokesperson said data centers make up about 18 percent of the utility's power use and that share could double by 2030. Also operating in the county is H5 Data Center in Nashville. The zoning appeals over the DC Blox site cannot be heard until the moratorium lapses in December.

Most of Wales's data center building is in the south, and most of it is Vantage Data Centers. Its Newport campus, on the site of a former LG semiconductor plant, has run since 2010 and is planned to reach 148 megawatts of power across three buildings; in August 2026 the AI cloud company Nebius agreed to lease space there. Vantage also has permission from the Vale of Glamorgan Council for a campus of up to 120 megawatts at the Bro Tathan business park in St Athan, and is developing a former Ford plant in Bridgend in phases through 2040.

The plans far outstrip what runs today. A July 2026 Welsh Parliament research briefing put Wales's data center capacity at 154 megawatts in 2024, and listed proposals of 148 and 150 megawatts in Cardiff, 200 in Newport, about 600 in Bridgend and 349 on Anglesey. Welsh planning policy, unlike England's and Scotland's, does not mention data centers at all, so councils are deciding them without specific guidance.

In the north, Anglesey County Council refused Carbon3.ai's plan to turn the former Octel bromine works at Amlwch Port, a 61-acre site empty since 2004, into an AI data center. Its decision notice of April 20, 2026, found "insufficient information has been submitted to demonstrate that the proposal will not harm the landscape, special designated sites, ecology, Welsh Water apparatus as well as the amenity of adjacent nearby residential properties."

Weld County's commissioners voted 5-0 on September 9, 2026 to approve a data center near Windsor for Global AI, even though the county had issued three stop-work orders for unpermitted construction there and the site's power and water supply were still unresolved. Rather than pause new data centers the way some other Colorado counties did in 2026, Weld adopted an ordinance keeping them to industrial or agricultural zones and requiring a site plan or special-review permit. A second, larger project, the 750-megawatt Cielo Hudson Data Center near the town of Hudson, is also proposed; no company name or other details have been made public.

Global AI, a New York company, bought the 438-acre former Kodak and Carestream Health campus near Windsor in late 2025 for about $15.6 million and plans a 41-acre data center starting at 27.5 megawatts, with talk of growing to a gigawatt, which would make it Colorado's largest. CPR News reported the county posted stop-work orders on May 7, June 11 and again before sending a formal order to abate on July 20. Global AI says it will operate the site with Nvidia and Humain, the Saudi-backed AI company.

CPR News found gaps in the power and water plans. Poudre Valley Rural Electric Association said it could supply only 35 megawatts through mid-2028, dropping after that; later phases would run on on-site Bloom fuel cells, for which the company had not yet filed state air permits. The site sits outside any water district: Windsor will only serve it if the land is annexed into town, and Greeley's water agreement with the former Kodak owner runs out in March 2027 unless Greeley, too, annexes the property. The Greeley City Council gave both sides 18 months to negotiate that.

At a daylong hearing, the county received more than 400 written comments. "People do not want to live next to data centers," said Marc Savela of Broe Real Estate Group, which has 2,000 homes planned nearby. Windsor resident Scott Simmons told CPR: "The noise, the power issues – it's just scary." The approval covers only the 41-acre first phase, not a gigawatt build-out, and requires closed-loop cooling, noise held to existing levels and a decommissioning bond.

Meta's Hyperion data center is being built on former farmland at Holly Ridge, an unincorporated community in Richland Parish between Rayville and Delhi, about 260 miles northwest of New Orleans. Fox 8 put the cost at $27 billion in May 2026; Meta has since announced it will expand the campus to 5 gigawatts of computing capacity. Entergy Louisiana is building the power supply beside it, and its vice president for hyperscale execution, Troy Heytens, told Fox 8 the combined site runs "about 5-6 miles long and a mile wide" and is "the biggest customer project that Entergy Louisiana has ever undertaken." He said the first gas plants at the Franklin Farms Power Station are due online by the end of 2028 and the data center by 2030.

The parish is feeling it. Tax assessor Emmett "Lee" Brown told Fox 8 that after state incentives Meta is expected to pay the parish $30 million in property tax over three years, against $22 million the parish collected in all of last year, and that a parish of about 20,000 people now has at least 4,000 more living and working there. "A rental that might've been $600-$700/month is now $2,500/month," he said. "So, it's not affordable for the people that were here." On power bills he said: "We've been assured by the Public Service Commission that the rate increases will not happen." Joyce Piercy, 81, said: "When Meta came in, they moved some of the folks out and put in the trailer parks. Well, they had to find a place to go and some of them couldn't afford that." KNOE has reported cracked roads and heavier truck traffic on state highways.

Water comes from the town of Delhi. Mayor Jesse Washington told KNOE in July that the town will keep supplying the site after the expansion, that Meta will pay for improvements and a new water treatment plant due next year, and that "rate payers will not be affected." Margie Vicknair-Pray of the Sierra Club said the data center will "definitely compete with the agriculture in the area."

The larger fight is over electricity. Regulators approved three Entergy gas plants for the project in 2025. In April 2026 Entergy asked the Louisiana Public Service Commission to approve seven more, four in Richland Parish and three in Pointe Coupee Parish, under a fast-track process, for ten plants in all. Heytens said Meta will cover construction costs and that customers will save money. Logan Burke of the Alliance for Affordable Energy said her group worries ratepayers could be left with the plants if Meta leaves: "they're either overpaying for speed, which we'll all be on the hook for in the long run, or they won't be able to make these deadlines." Earthjustice attorney Susan Stevens Miller said the compressed timeline makes "meaningful public participation and careful regulatory review far more difficult." Paul Arbaje, an energy analyst at the Union of Concerned Scientists, a party to the case, wrote that under Entergy's own numbers the plants would be only about 75% depreciated when Meta's 20-year contract ends, leaving roughly $3.4 billion that ratepayers could carry; that Entergy's projected benefit to other customers falls to $991 million, about 3.5%, if Meta leaves after 20 years, so a 3.5% rise in costs would erase it; and that the cost of the plants for the project's first phase had already risen in May from $3.9 billion to $4.4 billion. Meta said its data center represents an investment of more than $10 billion and will support over 500 operational jobs.

On August 12, 2026, three commissioners, Erik Skrmetta, Jean-Paul Coussan and Mike Francis, voted to quash a subpoena an administrative law judge had upheld that would have required Meta to document its investment, permanent jobs and electricity demand, according to the Union of Concerned Scientists, one of the parties that sought it. The commission's final decision on the seven plants is scheduled for December 16, 2026.

paragraphs: A $2 billion AI data center planned for the 140-acre former Tonawanda Coke site, on the Niagara River in the Town of Tonawanda, is on hold after developer Riverview Innovation and Technology Campus paused its application and the town passed its own moratorium. The proposed 500,000-square-foot building would need about 300 megawatts of power and a $50 million substation; developer Jon Williams has led an estimated $100 million cleanup of a site a local assemblyman calls "one of the most dangerously toxic properties in the United States." On August 3, 2026, the Town Board voted unanimously for a one-year moratorium on data centers of 20 megawatts or more.

Riverview asked to pause its application in June 2026 because of a backlog at the New York grid operator, which studies whether the system can carry a load that size; the company said it was not abandoning the site. Residents packed a June 3 planning board meeting: Jamie Moore warned that cooling systems "typically operate at 75 to 105 decibels or greater," and one speaker compared the site to Love Canal. State Senator Jeremy Zellner said the project would use "just about as much electricity as my entire district uses." In July Governor Kathy Hochul came to Tonawanda Town Hall to sign an executive order pausing new data centers above 50 megawatts for up to a year.

Town Supervisor John Flynn said Riverview's was the only data center application in the town and that "there is no back door" around the moratorium. Riverview said it would review the vote with legal counsel "to determine our path forward." Buffalo already has one operating data center, run by H5 Data Centers downtown; a planned Tesla Dojo supercomputer nearby at the RiverBend solar plant was scrapped.

Haskell County, about 50 miles north of Abilene, is where Google is building part of the $40 billion Texas expansion it announced in November 2025, filed under affiliates rather than Google's name. Data Center Dynamics reported in July 2026 that Housebound Group LLC had registered two buildings at 1362 Red Creek Road in the north of the county, Journey 1A and Journey 2A, each a $400 million project of 285,280 and 210,420 square feet, with construction started on April 1 and June 23, 2026.

A second Google-linked campus, Thelma, lies in the south of the county and is further along. A wastewater application for it describes five buildings, the first 280,000 square feet and a second 350,000; the research firm Aterio estimates its total power capacity at around 440 megawatts. The county approved abatements for Journey and Thelma in June 2025, and a third Google-linked campus, developed by Ascendant Site Solutions, received one in April 2026.

Crusoe, which built the Stargate campus for Oracle and OpenAI in Abilene, is next. County records show commissioners designated a reinvestment zone for it on April 28, 2026, for a project whose first phase is put at about $1 billion, with a ten-year abatement on each of up to seven phases; the executed agreement carries a Crusoe signature dated July 21, 2026.

The effects are showing up in nearby towns. Stamford, on the border of Haskell and Jones counties, is seeing multiple houses built at once for the first time since the 1980s, Mayor James Decker told KTXS in May, some bought by workers who could not find affordable housing in Abilene. "It's jarring. It's very jarring to suddenly realize that the focus of this AI data center rush is in your area," Decker said. "We don't want to be chewed up and spit out by the data center boom."

Hill County, about 55 miles south of Fort Worth, became the first Texas county to try a data center moratorium, and dropped it within weeks under a lawsuit. On May 12, 2026, commissioners voted 3-2 to pause new data center construction in unincorporated areas for up to a year. "The data center folks have found a sweet spot in the state that has limited regulations, limited enforcement, limited code, and they're coming faster than we can keep up with," Commissioner Jim Holcomb said. County Judge Shane Brassell told the Texas Tribune he knew of at least eight projects in the works, mostly by word of mouth about farmers selling land, because developers do not have to tell the county. County Attorney David Holmes warned before the vote: "You're damned if you and damned if you don't."

On May 27 a developer, RCM Hill LLC, sued the county in federal court in Austin for $100 million, saying it had contracts to buy more than 800 acres and that the county "exceeded its lawful powers"; Texas counties, unlike cities, generally have no zoning authority. On June 4 commissioners voted unanimously to rescind the moratorium and instead adopt a checklist data center developers must complete. Brassell still called the pause a success: "some projects that were less desirable, as far as maybe not the most honest — they left the county."

The largest project on record is in Hubbard. Nexus Data Centers, backed by the private equity firm Transition Equity Partners, has registered two buildings at 357 HCR 3372 with the state licensing agency, Apex DFW HB1 and HB2, each 491,380 square feet and $400 million, with construction running from January 2026 to early 2028. DCD reported that Nexus is targeting a 600-megawatt campus powered by natural gas on site, and that Google is reportedly backing it to serve Anthropic.

Inside Hillsboro, the county seat, the question is the city's own land. Provident Realty Advisors of Dallas has under contract just under 300 acres owned by the Hillsboro Economic Development Corporation on the old city airport north of town. Because the site is inside city limits and zoned heavy industrial, it cannot proceed without a development agreement approved by the city. A crowd, many opposed, filled a two-hour forum with City Manager Megan Henderson at Historic City Hall on April 28, the Hillsboro Reporter said; the contract's review period runs through November.

Where RCM Hill's project is located was not reported in what was read. KWTX and KERA articles not read.

paragraphs: Flexential's largest project yet is outside Dallas. On July 28, 2026 the company said it had bought 110 acres near Talty, in Kaufman County, Texas, for a three-building campus: a first 375,000-square-foot, 36 MW building, room for two more the same size, site work starting in early 2027 and first customers in late 2028. Flexential says it will use closed-loop cooling aimed at zero water use.

Talty officials told NBC 5 they have no say over the site, since the land left the city's extraterritorial jurisdiction earlier in 2026 after a landowner petition to the county. Neighboring Forney has directed staff to draft zoning that would bar new data centers inside its limits.

Flexential is a Colorado-based colocation company formed in 2017, when GI Partners bought ViaWest and merged it with Peak 10; Morgan Stanley's infrastructure fund became a co-owner in 2024. DataCenterDynamics reported in June 2026 that it runs 42 data centers in 18 US markets, about 3 million square feet, with more than 330 megawatts built and planned, and that it has raised an $800 million asset-backed loan with another $1.4 billion planned. CoreWeave took 13 MW at its Plano, Texas site in 2025.

CEO Ryan Mallory told DataCenterDynamics that wholesale deals run 1 to 18 MW, with growth concentrated in Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Hillsboro, Nashville, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. He said Flexential is chasing 22MW to 72MW deals rather than multi-gigawatt campuses, including a 22MW data center in the Parker area of Denver and a 27MW facility in Hillsboro, Oregon, its fifth site there. He said reactions from residents and officials have been a mixed bag, including complaints about water rationing and brownouts.

Windstream is a Little Rock, Arkansas telecom company that sells rural broadband and wholesale fiber, and it is on this site for its network buildings rather than for any large new data center. It sold its data center business to TierPoint in 2015 for $575 million. What remains are switch sites and colocation rooms inherited from the phone companies it absorbed: Windstream was formed in 2006 from Alltel's local telephone business and Valor Communications. The Windstream site listed on this page is a colocation building at Innsbrook in Henrico County, Virginia, that carries the name of the former carrier Cavalier Telephone.

In May 2024 Windstream agreed to merge back into Uniti Group, the Little Rock fiber and tower landlord that was spun out of Windstream in 2015 and had been its landlord since. Under the deal Uniti shareholders took about 62 percent of the combined company, and Windstream shareholders received $425 million in cash and $575 million of preferred equity. The merged company now concentrates on fiber rather than on the buildings this page is about.

The company has been selling the real estate under those buildings. In August 2024 JLL marketed eight switch and data center sites in seven states, from Lexington, Kentucky to Hobbs, New Mexico, totaling 379,000 square feet and leased to a tenant DCD identified as likely Windstream through 2034, with $5.7 million a year in rent. JLL described the Lexington site as the switch and data center hub for the tenant's east coast operations.

No news found about the Innsbrook building itself. The Cavalier Innsbrook name, Innsbrook and Henrico County come from this site's own project listing, not from a cited article.

paragraphs: The Central Denmark Region's best-known data center is Apple's at Foulum, in an industrial park about 4.5 kilometres outside Viborg. It was announced at a press conference in Viborg in February 2015 by the then mayor, Torsten Nielsen, and a government minister, and from the start it was sold locally on its waste heat, which was said to be enough to warm not only Viborg but much of central Jutland. Apple's own 2025 environmental report, as cited by Computer Weekly, put the operating load at only about 7 megawatts.

The heat took a decade to arrive. Danish taxes and a price cap on industrial waste heat kept district heating companies from buying it, and the Danish parliament agreed to scrap the cap in January 2025. The Viborg district heating company, Viborg Varme, which supplies about 20,000 homes, proposed spending 266 million kroner on an energy hub and a 4.5-kilometre transmission line from Foulum, also taking heat from Energinet's transformer station next to the data center. TV Midtvest reported the heat was expected to cover at least half of Viborg's demand at first, and the utility's chairman, Kristian Brøns Nielsen, said it would cut an ordinary house's bill by 3,000 to 4,000 kroner a year. Chief executive Morten Abildgaard told Computer Weekly in May 2025 that at full build-out the site "will produce far more heat than we could ever use", but the utility wants several heat sources rather than depending on one.

What happens next in the region depends on national grid politics. In March 2026 the state grid operator Energinet paused new connection agreements after requests reached about 60 gigawatts against a national peak load of about 7 GW; data centers account for roughly 14 GW of that queue, Energinet told CNBC. After the election, climate and energy minister Samira Nawa blamed foreign data centers owned by "American tech giants", and in July 2026 an emergency bill went to public consultation that would give data centers lowest priority for scarce grid capacity unless they serve functions such as health, defence or emergency services. Computer Weekly reported the plan had the backing of parties holding 80 per cent of parliament. Henrik Hansen of the Danish Data Center Industry association told CNBC the queue had become a "fantasy" and needed cleaning up. The Danish Energy Agency had already cut its forecast in December, Computer Weekly reported, assuming two-thirds of queued projects would never be built, and an industry association analysis put installed data center capacity at 1.2 GW in 2030 despite 15 to 20 GW in the queue.

No other Central Denmark Region projects found in the reporting read. Full-article re-read (after the reader's 6,000-character truncation was fixed) added the Energy Agency forecast cut and the 1.2 GW projection from the tail of Computer Weekly's emergency-plan story.

paragraphs: Egypt's data centers are small so far, and most are around Cairo. The largest, Telecom Egypt's International Data Center in the Smart Village in West Cairo, has about 4.6 megawatts of power. The biggest announced project is a $250 million data center at Maadi Technology Park in Cairo by the UAE's Khazna and Egypt's Benya Group, first announced in 2023 at 25 megawatts, expandable to 50, and due to be finished within three years.

Other plans are earlier still. In October 2024, Egypt's Intro Technology and Oman Data Park signed a memorandum of understanding for the Kemet Data Center, a $450 million, two-phase facility in the Suez Canal Economic Zone. In September 2026, Communications Minister Raafat Hindi met Heka Data and an unnamed US group of developers about a large data center and AI hub; the size and phases were still being discussed, and the ministry said such a hub needs reliable power.

Egypt's telecom regulator is pitching the country's undersea cables and spare electricity. Ahmed Yehia Hegazy of the National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority told Arab Finance the industry "is deeply tied to electricity," adding: "A single data center can consume as much power as an entire industrial zone."

Cairo is where Egypt's data centers are concentrated; DCD noted in 2024 that Telecom Egypt, Orange, GPX and Etisalat all have facilities in the capital. The planned step up in scale is at Maadi Technology Park, where the UAE's Khazna Data Centers, enlarged by a merger with G42 and Etisalat Group announced in 2021, partnered with the Egyptian IT firm Benya Group in 2023 on a $250 million data center of 25 MW, expandable to 50 MW, across 40,000 square metres. It was billed as Egypt's first hyperscale facility and the first in a series; construction was to start in 2023 with completion "within three years". Benya's chairman, Ahmed Mekky, said it would serve African and Middle Eastern countries as well as Egypt. No reporting found in 2026 confirms how far it has been built.

The largest operating site in the city is Telecom Egypt's Regional Data Hub. Its first phase delivered 2.5 MW in 2021 and was full by 2022; a second phase of about 4.6 MW was due in 2025, though w.media reported the company had not publicly confirmed it is fully running. In September 2025 Telecom Egypt agreed to sell 75 to 80 per cent of the hub to Helios Investment Partners at a valuation of $230 million to $260 million. On July 15, 2026 its board dropped the deal, citing unmet conditions in the term sheet including some tied to third parties, and said it would instead move its data center business into a wholly owned subsidiary. Telecom Egypt engineer Hossam Badawy told Arab Finance that Cairo is becoming attractive to cloud providers because of its connectivity, with Alexandria the gateway for international traffic.

Smart Village is left off this page because it sits in Giza governorate, not Cairo.

paragraphs: County Meath's biggest data center fight was over a second campus at Clonee, and it lasted four years. EngineNode, an Irish company founded in 2018 by two former Eir executives, applied in November 2019 for a campus of four two-storey data buildings, about 92,100 square metres, and a substation on a 24.5-hectare site at Bracetown and Gunnocks, just north of Meta's. Meath County Council approved it on condition EngineNode pay €1.85 million towards the new Bracetown link road, which the company tried to challenge. An Taisce and Friends of the Irish Environment appealed, arguing Ireland already hosted a disproportionate share of western Europe's data centers and more would strain the national grid, where EirGrid projected data centers could reach 29 per cent of demand by 2028. An Bord Pleanála granted permission in July 2021. The planning inspector, Karla McBride, said she was satisfied the energy issue would "ultimately" be addressed as Ireland moved towards 70 per cent renewable electricity by 2030.

Neighbors Mannix and Amy Coyne, who run an equine business from their home at Bracetown, then took the decision to the High Court, arguing the 180 MW campus would produce an estimated 1 per cent of Ireland's annual carbon dioxide emissions and breached their constitutional right to a healthy environment, and separately challenged the substation and grid connection. On July 21, 2023 Mr Justice David Holland rejected every ground in both cases. During the planning fight, An Bord Pleanála also found that EngineNode's plans included a roundabout and road across Meta's land without its permission.

Clonee's first data center was Facebook's, now Meta's, which opened in 2018 and which Silicon Republic described in 2021 as a €300 million campus; Meta says it is powered by renewable energy through a deal to use Brookfield Renewable's Irish wind farms. Meta has also run a community grants programme in the county since 2018 and says it has given more than €4.8 million to 186 projects; its ninth round opened in September 2026.

Dropped: Meta Clonee floor area and expansion figures (directory/preview only); the €2.29M rail contribution (preview only). BreakingNews.ie returned a Cloudflare challenge. The grant figures are Meta's own, attributed.

paragraphs: Israel wants to be an AI infrastructure hub and has run out of grid to do it with. On July 20, 2026 the Electricity Authority froze new grid connection applications from data centers of 8 megawatts or more for 140 days, until early December, calling it an "emergency brake". Calcalist reported that the grid operator, Noga, had received about 19,000 MW of new data center requests in two months on top of a backlog of about 8,000 MW, for roughly 27,000 MW in all, against average national consumption of about 9,000 MW and a peak of about 17,000 MW in August 2025. The authority said existing commitments to connect about 1.5 gigawatts of data centers already use up the power sector's planned generation capacity through 2035, and warned that more could raise natural gas use and consumer prices. "These are insane numbers, and there is no scenario in which we can catch up with such demand," a senior electricity official told Calcalist.

The rush followed government policy. DCD reported that the Knesset in February passed the National Cyber Defense Bill, which defined data centers as national infrastructure to strip away planning and construction constraints, and in June the government approved a national plan to accelerate AI. During the freeze the authority, the energy ministry and Noga are drafting criteria to separate serious projects from speculative ones; the authority had already been working on a rule that would make developers pay millions of shekels a year to hold a place in the queue. Noga said the question is "how it is right to allocate a limited public and infrastructure resource among all the needs of the economy." At least one developer, VisionWave, dropped plans for a hyperscale site in Israel, citing the pause, and shares of the data center developer Mega Or fell 6 per cent on the announcement. Noga said its development plan dated from 2021, when data center demand was far lower, though it had still approved about 2,000 MW of connections, and warned that more would push natural gas use beyond forecasts at a time when Israel has committed to large exports, including the Leviathan partnership's deal with Egypt valued at about $35 billion.

The largest operator on the ground is Amazon Web Services. It opened its Israel cloud region in August 2023 after winning, with Google, the government's $1.2 billion Project Nimbus cloud tender; local press placed its data centers at Tnuvot in the Sharon region, at Shoham, and at the Har Tov industrial park near Beit Shemesh. In November 2025 Globes reported that AWS had signed a letter of intent to lease a 42-dunam (10.5-acre) lot near Tnuvot, east of Netanya, where a 60,000-square-meter data center of 35 to 40 MW could be built, roughly doubling its processing capacity in Israel. DCD reported in June 2026 that Crusoe plans to invest about $10 billion in Israeli data centers over 10 to 15 years through leases.
